changes.summary: In its Cabinet of Graphic Art, the Musée d'Orsay is exhibiting a selection of 19th-century drawings inspired by the Mediterranean’s majestic cedars. Through works by Guillaumet, Lévy-Dhurmer and Belly, acquaint yourself with the beauty of these emblematic trees. The cedar forests so dear to the poets Alphonse de Lamartine and Stéphane Mallarmé also inspired the 19th century’s graphic artists. Conical when it is young, the cedar tree takes a hundred years for it to attain the emblematic shape we know it by. Its “gigantic stages” take shape among the Northern Algerian desert’s fig trees, flowering hawthorns and white lilies that Gustave Guillaumet depicted in ink, charcoal and pastel on tracing paper and sheets of violet-, blue- and grey-tinted paper. Lucien Lévy-Dhurmer used blue crayons to sketch the Atlas cedars’ slender outlines, while Léon Belly filled the pages of his sketchbooks with them during his journey from the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea.
